title: Repeating transformations and finite-state patterns
transcript: A finite-state rule has only a limited set of possible situations. Once the same full state occurs again, the same rule repeats everything that follows. Sometimes there is a short starting path before a loop. Count that path separately from the repeating part.

In AMC practice, a repeating transformation might turn a pointer, change a colour or move a mark. Record the complete state between steps. A Mawa style investigation can compare loops from different starting states. Ask which states repeat and which appear only once.
A pointer begins facing north. Turn it clockwise by a quarter turn twenty-one times. Where does it point? Count how many quarter turns bring it back to north.
Four turns make one complete revolution. Dividing twenty-one by four leaves one extra turns. Apply those extra turns from north. The pointer ends facing east.
On each press, one dial moves to its next position in a cycle of two. A second dial moves in a cycle of five. After how many presses is the full starting pair first restored?
The first dial resets at multiples of two, and the second at multiples of five. The first positive common reset occurs after ten presses. The state consists of both dials, not just one.

A machine starts at state one. It moves up through the numbered states until eight. From there its next state is four, and it follows the same rule forever. The starting state is at step zero. Where is it after sixty-five moves?

At step three the machine first reaches four, the first state of the loop. The earlier states do not recur. The loop has five states. From the loop entry, there are sixty-two more moves to make. Divide by the loop length. The remainder is two. Move that far from the first loop state to reach six.
Each complete loop returns to state four. After twelve complete loops, we are back at that state at step sixty-three. Take two more moves from there to reach state six at step sixty-five.

A displayed position may not capture the full situation. Include any second dial or change in the rule that affects the next move. The lead-in happens only once. Subtract its length before dividing by the size of the loop.

List the first few complete states and name the next-step rule. Stop when a full state repeats. Separate the first visit to the loop from later laps. Check whether your indexing is by moves from zero or by states from one.
